Empirical Research Plan:  Compulsory‐Schooling–Induced Education and Civic Engagement 

========================================================
1. Identification Strategy
========================================================
Method:  Two–stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental-variables design that exploits staggered changes in state compulsory–schooling laws (CSLs).

Why IV?  
• The research question is the causal effect of an endogenous variable (own schooling) on civic outcomes.  
• Schooling is correlated with unobserved ability, motivation, family background, etc. – OLS is biased.  
• CSL reforms created exogenous, plausibly unconfounded variation in years of schooling by state × birth-cohort.  
• The staggered timing delivers cross-sectional and inter-temporal variation while allowing rich fixed effects and clustered inference.

Relation to other methods: The same staggered reforms could be cast as a DID/event-study, but because the endogenous regressor is continuous and we are interested in the causal effect of education itself, the IV formulation is cleaner (education = treatment; CSL = instrument).

========================================================
2. Treatment and Control
========================================================
Treatment variable (endogenous regressor):  
  EDUC_i  = completed years of schooling of individual i (continuous).

Instrument (Z_{s,c}):  
  “Exposed-to-higher-CSL” indicator equal to 1 if individual i was born in state s and cohort c (defined by year of birth) that, by age 14, was subject to a CSL requiring > k years (typically >8 or >9) OR raising the minimum leaving age (e.g., from 14 to 16). Alternative: continuous instrument = statutory minimum years required.

Control group:  
  Individuals born in the same state(s) and surrounding cohorts **prior** to the CSL change, plus individuals in other states that did not change their CSL in that year. In 2SLS the control group enters implicitly through the fixed effects.

Treatment timing:  
  Event date = year when new CSL became binding for a given birth cohort (year of birth + compulsory-schooling-age threshold).  
  We code a cohort as “treated” if their 14th birthday occurred in or after the first full school year under the new law.

No running variable – this is not an RDD.

========================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
========================================================
A1. Relevance (First-stage): CSL reforms materially increased completed schooling.  
  – Plausible: a large literature documents strong first stages of 0.2–0.4 years per one-year increase in compulsory schooling.

A2. Independence / Exogeneity: Conditional on state and cohort fixed effects (and covariates), CSL exposure is independent of unobserved determinants of civic engagement.  
  – Institutional context: Laws were passed for labor-market or child-welfare reasons, not civic-engagement motives; reforms are largely orthogonal to unobserved individual civic preferences.

A3. Exclusion: CSL affects civic engagement only through education, not via other channels (e.g., contemporaneous child-labor regulation, time in school spilling over into civic instruction).  
  – Some concern: schools may directly teach civics; still, main mechanism is through additional schooling. Will test with robustness checks and placebo outcomes.

A4. Monotonicity: Nobody reduces their schooling because of a stricter CSL (no “defiers”).  
  – Highly plausible: raising the minimum years cannot legally induce someone to drop out earlier.

A5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): One individual’s treatment status does not change another’s civic outcome in a way that biases 2SLS (peer effects assumed small relative to sample).  
  – Reasonable at national scale.

========================================================
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
========================================================
T1. Concurrent state policy changes (e.g., voting laws, welfare policy) correlated with CSL passage.  
  Mitigation:  
   • Include state-specific linear and quadratic birth-cohort trends.  
   • Control for time-varying state covariates (e.g., unemployment, unionization, school spending).  
   • Event-study falsification: check civic outcomes for cohorts too old to be affected (“lead” dummies).

T2. Selective migration: Families may move to avoid/seek tougher CSLs.  
  Mitigation:  
   • Code treatment based on state of birth, not state of residence at survey.  
   • Show robustness to restricting sample to non-movers (same birth-state and survey-state).  
   • Compare movers’ observables pre-reform to detect selection.

T3. Measurement error in schooling or civic outcomes dilutes first stage or violates exclusion.  
  Mitigation:  
   • Use multiple schooling measures (years, degree dummies).  
   • Instrument strength checks (F-stat >10).  
   • Use alternative civic outcomes (e.g., volunteered last year, group membership) to confirm patterns.

========================================================
5. R Code Outline
========================================================
```r
####################  (1) Load packages  ####################
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast 2SLS & DID
library(haven)       # if GSS in .dta
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

####################  (2) Load data  #########################
gss <- read_csv("gss_clean.csv")              # assume already harmonised
csl <- read_csv("csl_state_year.csv")         # min school-leaving age by state & year

####################  (3) Create birth-cohort exposure vars ##
gss <- gss %>% 
  mutate(birth_year = year - age,           # survey year – age
         state = state_fips) %>% 
  left_join(csl, by = c("state")) %>% 
  mutate(age14_year = birth_year + 14,
         csl_required_yrs = ifelse(age14_year >= law_year, new_min_grade, old_min_grade),
         z_exposed = as.integer(csl_required_yrs >= 10))   # “treated” if ≥10 years required

####################  (4) Outcomes & controls ################
gss <- gss %>% 
  mutate(educ = educyrs,
         voter_reg = as.integer(voter_reg == "Yes"),
         voted_last = as.integer(vote_pres == "Yes"),
         civic_partic = rowMeans(select(., org_union:org_charity), na.rm = TRUE), # example
         female = sex == "Female",
         black = race == "Black")

####################  (5) 2SLS main specification  ###########
# specification: Civic_i = beta * educ_hat + X_i + state_FE + cohort_FE + e_i
ivs <- feols(voter_reg ~ 1 | educ ~ z_exposed |         # outcome | first-stage ~ instrument
               female + black + age + I(age^2) |        # controls
               state + birth_year,                      # two-way fixed effects
             data = gss, cluster = ~state)
summary(ivs, stage = 1)   # print 1st and 2nd stage

####################  (6) Robustness: Alt instrument #########
gss <- gss %>% 
  mutate(z_alt = csl_required_yrs)                     # continuous CSL
ivs_alt <- feols(voter_reg ~ 1 | educ ~ z_alt | 
                   female + black + age + I(age^2) | state + birth_year,
                 data = gss, cluster = ~state)
etable(ivs, ivs_alt, se = "cluster")

####################  (7) Event-study placebo (leads)  #######
gss <- gss %>% 
  mutate(lead2 = as.integer(birth_year %in% (law_year - 3):(law_year - 1)))
placebo <- feols(voter_reg ~ lead2 +                          # should be ≈0
                   female + black + age + I(age^2) | state + birth_year,
                 data = gss, cluster = ~state)
summary(placebo)
```
(Replace variable names with actual GSS harmonised codes.)

========================================================
6. Expected Results
========================================================
Economic theory and prior evidence (e.g., Milligan, Moretti & Oreopoulos 2004) suggest that additional schooling:  
• raises political knowledge, efficacy, and the probability of voting/registration;  
• boosts participation in community groups.

Magnitude: A one-year increase in schooling is expected to raise the probability of voter registration by roughly 2–4 ppt and actual voting by 1.5–3 ppt. Similar or slightly larger effects are plausible for broad civic-participation indices.

========================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
========================================================
C1: Instrument relevance (F-stat >10) …………… 1  
C2: Independence / random assignment ………… 0.8 (laws exogenous, but politics?)  
C3: Exclusion restriction …………………………… 0.7 (other channels possible)  
C4: Monotonicity (no defiers) ……………………… 1  
C5: SUTVA (no cross-unit spillovers) …………… 1  

Overall ≈ 4.5 / 5 (reasonably strong but exclusion assumption deserves scrutiny).
